lead: Today’s readings look at life inside the community of believers. John says that nobody can claim to be in the light while hating a brother or sister. Matthew gives Jesus’ patient steps for winning back one who has sinned, and promises his presence where two or three gather in his name. Love in the Church is not a mood. It has a practice, and the Lord himself stands in the middle of it.

r.h: The old commandment that is new
set: 1 John has no greeting and names no author; tradition links it with the apostle John, and it clearly comes from the same world as the Fourth Gospel. Many scholars date it to the end of the first century. A group has left the community (2:19), and the writer gives his readers tests of true faith: do you keep his commandments, and do you love one another? Just before this passage he says that whoever claims to abide in Christ “ought to walk just as he walked” (2:6).
str: v. 7: an old commandment, the one you have heard from the beginning.
v. 8: yet it is new, because the true light is already shining.
vv. 9–11: the test: hating means darkness, and loving means light.
kw: The one Jesus gave at the supper: “love one another” (John 13:34). It is old because it was heard from the beginning, and new because Christ has lived it to the end.
The same verb returns in 2:17: “the world and its desire are passing away”. Darkness is still around, but its time is ending. The present tense gives hope.
The word used in v. 10. It first meant a trap or something that trips a person. One who loves does not trip over his own feet, and he does not trip others.
vv: because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.
It is a picture of early dawn. The writer does not claim that all is bright. He says which way the day is moving.
Whoever says, “I am in the light,” while hating a brother or sister, is still in the darkness.

Fine words about faith cannot cover hatred. The NRSV’s “brother or sister” represents the Greek “brother”, a member of the Christian family, and the Gospel of the same tradition shows God’s love reaching the whole world (John 3:16).
Whoever loves a brother or sister lives in the light, and in such a person there is no cause for stumbling.
The verb is “abides”, a key word of this letter. Love is more than an act. It is where a person lives.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus makes charity the new commandment, and that by loving his own to the end he shows the Father’s love (CCC 1823). St Augustine preached ten homilies on this letter, and for him its one subject is charity (in substance). In the Great Fast the question is direct: is there someone I will not speak to? My fast and my prayer should begin there.

r.h: Where two or three are gathered
set: Chapter 18 is the fourth of the five great discourses in Matthew, on life in the community. Just before this, the shepherd goes after one lost sheep (18:12–14). Just after, Peter asks how often he must forgive, and Jesus tells the parable of the unforgiving servant (18:21–35). The steps of today’s passage stand between mercy and mercy, and must be read in that light.
str: v. 16: take one or two others.
v. 17: tell the Church, and the last step if all is refused.
vv. 19–20: prayer in agreement, and the Lord’s presence.
kw: In the Gospels this word appears only here and in Matthew 16:18. It is the Greek word used in the Greek Old Testament for the assembly of Israel.
“You have regained that one.” It is a merchant’s word: a brother is treasure. The whole aim of correction is to win him back, not to win the argument.
The Greek behind our word “symphony” (v. 19). It means more than a shared opinion. Voices are joined in one request.
vv: If another member of the church sins against you, go and point out the fault when the two of you are alone.

The first step asks for two things: courage and discretion. It is easier to tell others than to tell the person. A note on the text: some important old manuscripts lack “against you” (the NRSV notes this), and the POC follows that shorter wording.
let such a one be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector.

This is the last step, and it should be read with care. In Matthew Jesus eats with tax collectors (9:10–11) and calls one of them to be an apostle (9:9). It marks a real break, and it also says where the Church must begin again: with a call to come back.
Truly I tell you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.

“Bind” and “loose” were terms used by Jewish teachers for forbidding and permitting, and for imposing or lifting a ban. Here “you” is plural. The authority given to Peter (16:19) is also given to the apostles with him.
For where two or three are gathered in my name, I am there among them.

Matthew’s Gospel is framed by this promise: “God is with us” (1:23) and “I am with you always” (28:20). A Jewish saying in the Mishnah speaks of God’s presence resting on two who study the Law together; Jesus says this of himself.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the office of binding and loosing given to Peter was also given to the college of the apostles united with its head (CCC 1444), and it links this power to reconciliation with the Church (CCC 1445). Among the ways Christ is present to his Church, it names the gathering in his name, and above all the Eucharistic species (CCC 1373; Sacrosanctum Concilium 7).

qa: Why does the English say “sins against you” while the Malayalam only says “does wrong”?

Some important old manuscripts of Matthew do not have the words “against you” (the NRSV notes this), and the POC follows that shorter wording. With them, the passage is about a personal injury. Without them, it is about any serious sin we notice in a fellow believer. In both, the first step is the same: go quietly, in love.
study: Is there someone I have talked about to others, when I should have gone to speak to that person alone?
Whom in my family or parish could I pray with this week, trusting the promise of Matthew 18:20?
